ety: The origin of this colloquialism seems to have its roots in mid-19th century horseracing. By the late 19th century the phrase was being used in non-racing contexts to mean 'with no trouble at all.'

s.def: Able to survive adverse growing conditions, especially frost.
ex: A hardy plant is one that can withstand the extremes of climate, such as frost.
The oat is hardier than wheat, and ripens in higher latitudes.

s.def: Brave and resolute.
Impudent.
Anything, especially a plant, that is hardy.
A blacksmith's fuller or chisel, having a square shank for insertion into a square hole in an anvil.
A hardy hole.

ety: From Middle English hare, from Old English hara (“hare”), from Proto-West Germanic *hasō ~ *haʀ-, from Proto-Germanic *hesô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱh₂s-én-; possibly related to or influenced by Proto-Germanic *haswaz (“grey”). Cognates See also West Frisian hazze, Dutch haas, German Hase, Norwegian and Swedish hare, Icelandic heri), Old English hasu, Middle High German heswe (“pale, dull”); also Welsh cannu (“to whiten”), ceinach (“hare”), Latin cānus (“white”), cascus (“old”), Old Prussian…

s.def: The meat from this animal.
ex: Ashe bit absent-mindedly into a piece of hare and swore mildly when he burned his tongue.
Hare is another delicious meat – it’s more ‘steaky’, darker and richer than rabbit.
In Milan, jugged hare is flavoured with grated chocolate, which adds colour and depth to the sauce.

s.def: Any of several plant-eating mammals of the genus Lepus, similar to a rabbit, but larger and with longer ears.
ex: The hare has a reputation for exciting desire. Hare soup is credited with a particular aphrodisiac value.

s.def: The player in a paperchase, or hare and hounds game, who leaves a trail of paper to be followed.
To move swiftly.
ex: But Wales somehow snaffled possession for fly-half Jones to send half-back partner Mike Phillips haring away with Stoddart in support.

s.def: To excite; to tease, or worry; to harry.
Grey, hoary; grey-haired, venerable (of people).
ex: a hare old man

s.def: Cold, frosty (of weather).

ety: From Middle English harebelle, equivalent to hare + bell.

s.def: A perennial flowering plant, Campanula rotundifolia, native to the Northern Hemisphere, with blue, bell-like flowers.
ex: How Snow-drops cold, and blue-eyed Harebells blend / Their tender tears, as o'er the stream they bend […].

s.def: foxglove

ety: From hare + brained.

s.def: Absurd, foolish or stupid.
Frivolous and silly; featherbrained or scatterbrained; stupid.

ety: From hare + lip.

s.def: A congenital malformation of the upper lip, reminiscent of the mouth of a hare.
To curse (as if by causing a harelip),
ex: I don't care if it harelips the governor.
I'm gonna get them doors open if it harelips everybody on Bear Creek!

ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حرم (harem) (whence Turkish harem), from Arabic حَرَم (ḥaram, “something prohibited; sanctuary, women”); and later also from حَرِيم (ḥarīm) with same meaning, both from حَرُمَ (ḥaruma, “be forbidden or unlawful”). Doublet of haram and herem.

s.def: The private section of a Muslim household forbidden to male strangers.
A group of someone's girlfriends, wives and/or concubines in a polygamous household.

A group of female animals (cows) herded and controlled by a male animal (bull) of that species for breeding purposes. Such behaviour is exhibited by bovids including cattle and buffalo as well as moose, elephants, seals (including elephant seals), sea lions, and baboons.
A group of female birds mated to or associated with a breeding male.
Any significant number of women together as a group; a bevy.
A genre of anime and manga in which a man is the love interest of three or more women.

ety: The head of the grass resembles a hare's tail.

s.def: Lagurus ovatus, an annual grass.

ety: Borrowed from French haricot (“bean”).

s.def: Synonym of common bean.
A stew of lamb and vegetables.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic حَرِيرَة (ḥarīra)

s.def: A thickened, tomato-based North African soup, popular during Ramadan.
ex: Like most hariras, this Berber version is finished off with a thickening agent to develop the proper velvety texture.

ety: From Middle English herken, herkien, from Old English *hercian, *heorcian, *hiercian, from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀikōn, *hauʀukōn, derived ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną (“to hear”) + formative/intensive -k (see also the related hīeran, whence English hear). Equivalent to hear + -k. Cognate with Scots herk (“to hark”), North Frisian harke (“to hark”), West Frisian harkje (“to listen”), obsolete Dutch horken (“to hark, listen to”), Middle Low German horken (“to hark”), German horche…

s.def: To listen attentively.
ex: But harke, I heare the footing of a man.
Hark! the herald angels sing / Glory to the new born King
Loud voices and a renewed uproar were raised in front of the boarding-house[…] "'Tis Missis Murphy's voice," said Mrs. McCaskey, harking.

s.def: A whisper

ety: See hearken

s.def: Alternative spelling of hearken: to hear, to listen, to have regard.
ex: How, then, am I mad? Harken! and observe how healthily—how calmly I can tell you the whole story.

s.def: To hark back, to return or revert (to a subject, etc.), to allude to, to evoke, to long or pine for (a past event or era).
ex: Bell argued that the manual approach was "backwards," and harkened to a primitive age where humans used gesture and pantomime.

ety: Cognate with Middle Low German herle, Low German harle, Saterland Frisian harrel (“hemp fibre”).

s.def: A fibre, especially a fibre of hemp or flax, or an individual fibre of a feather.
ex: She pushed her fingers under the cream lace, into the ginger harl of spun glass.

s.def: A barb, or barbs, of a fine large feather, as of a peacock or ostrich, used in dressing artificial flies.
ex: Should it be desired, however, to run the hackle all over the body, it may be tied on along with the peacock's harls.

s.def: To surface a building using a slurry of pebbles or stone chips which is then cured using a lime render.
To drag along the ground.
To drag oneself along.
To troll for fish.
The act of dragging.
A small quantity; a scraping of anything.

ety: From earlier Harlicken, from Middle French Harlequin (in Italian Arlecchino, the name of a popular servant character in commedia dell'arte plays), from Old French Harlequin, Halequin, Herlequin, Hellequin, Hierlekin, Hellekin (a demon, malevolent spirit), probably of Germanic origin, connected to the Old English figure of *Herla Cyning (“King Herla”, a mythical figure identified with Woden) or possibly to Old Frisian helle kin, Old English helle cyn, Old Norse heljar kyn (“the kindred of Hell”)…

s.def: A pantomime fool, typically dressed in colorful checkered clothes, used as a stock character in commedia dell'arte and other genres.
ex: Motives are like harlequins—there is always a second dress beneath their first.

s.def: A greenish-chartreuse color.
A harlequin duck.
Any of various riodinid butterflies of the genera Taxila and Praetaxila.
Brightly colored, especially in a pattern like that of a harlequin clown's clothes.
Of a greenish-chartreuse color.
To remove or conjure away, as if by a harlequin's trick.
ex: And kitten, if the humour hit / Has harlequin'd away the fit.

s.def: To make sport by playing ludicrous tricks.

ety: From Middle English harlot, from Old French harlot, herlot, arlot (“vagabond; tramp”), of obscure origin. Likely to be ultimately of Germanic origin, either from a derivation of *harjaz (“army; camp; warrior; military leader”) or from a diminutive of *karilaz (“man; fellow”). Compare English carlot.

s.def: A female prostitute.
ex: The bastard of a harlot, born in a brothel, suckled on gin, and familiar from earliest infancy with all the bestialities of debauch,[…]
He was stopped by a painted harlot, who put her hand on his arm; he pushed her violently away with brutal words.
O fine religious, decent folk, / In Virtue’s flaunting gold and scarlet, / I sneer between two puffs of smoke,— / Give me the publican and harlot.

s.def: A female who is considered promiscuous.
A churl; a common man; a person, male or female, of low birth, especially one given to low conduct.
ex: By suche ydle and wicked harlottes the enheritaunce of Christe is troden vnder fote.

s.def: To play the harlot; to practice lewdness.
ex: […] they that spend their youth in loitering, bezzling, and harlotting, their studies in unprofitable questions, and barbarous sophistry

s.def: Wanton; lewd; low; base.
ex: The intellection in it, kiddo—the intellection.... That most harlot of harlots... talking of me, laughing at me... I'll kill her....

ety: From harlot + -ry.

s.def: The trade of a harlot; prostitution.
ex: Harlotry, wine, and new wine take away the understanding.
Harlotry, wine, and new wine enslave the heart.

ety: From Middle English harm, herm, from Old English hearm, from Proto-West Germanic *harm, from Proto-Germanic *harmaz (“harm; shame; pain”). Cognate with Dutch harm (“harm”), German Harm (“harm”), Danish harme (“indignation, resentment”), Icelandic harmur (“sorrow, grief”), Swedish harm (“anger, indignation, harm”).

s.def: Physical injury; hurt; damage.
ex: No harm came to my possessions.
You can do a lot of harm to someone if you kick them in the teeth.

s.def: Emotional or figurative hurt.
ex: Although not physically injured in the car accident, she received some psychological harm.

s.def: Detriment; misfortune.
ex: I wish him no harm.

s.def: That which causes injury, damage, or loss.
ex: We, ignorant of ourselves, / Beg often our own harms.

s.def: To damage, hurt, or injure something, usually an inanimate object.
ex: Will justice and conscience of society not be harmed if people avoid the truth?

ety: From Arabic حَرْمَل (ḥarmal).

s.def: Peganum harmala, a perennial plant of the family Nitrariaceae.

ety: From Middle English harmful, from Old English *hearmful (suggested by hearmfullīċ (“harmful; hurtful”)), equivalent to harm + -ful. Cognate with German harmvoll, Danish harmfuld, Swedish harmfull.

s.def: Causing or likely to cause harm or damage; injurious.
ex: Wear a hat to protect your skin from harmful sunlight.
Smoking is harmful to the lungs.
Burning fossil fuels is harmful to the environment.

ety: Etymology tree English harmful Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English harmfulness From harmful + -ness.

s.def: The characteristic of being harmful.
ex: Once his word was pledged, he was safe: otherwise there was no limit to his capacity for wilful harmfulness.

ety: From Middle English harmles, from Old English *hearmlēas, from Proto-Germanic *harmalausaz (“without harm; harmless”), equivalent to harm + -less. Cognate with German harmlos (“harmless”), Danish harmløs (“harlmess”), Swedish harmlös (“harmless”).

s.def: Incapable of causing harm or danger; safe.
ex: Near-synonyms: benign, innocuous, innocent, undamaging, nonthreatening, unthreatening
This snake looks nearly the same as its poisonous cousin but is harmless.

s.def: Not intended to harm; inoffensive.
ex: His humor can be annoying but is harmless.

s.def: Unharmed.

ety: From Latin harmonicus, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονικός (harmonikós), from ἁρμονία (harmonía, “harmony”). By surface analysis, harmony + -ic. Doublet of armónico.

s.def: Pertaining to harmony.
Pleasant to hear; harmonious; melodious.
ex: harmonic twang of leather, horn, and brass.

s.def: Used to characterize various mathematical entities or relationships supposed to bear some resemblance to musical consonance.
ex: The harmonic polar line of an inflection point of a cubic curve is the component of the polar conic other than the tangent line.

s.def: Recurring periodically.
Exhibiting or applying constraints on what vowels (e.g. front/back vowels only) may be found near each other and sometimes in the entire word.
Of or relating to a generation an even number of generations distant from a particular person.
A component frequency of the signal of a wave that is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.
The place where, on a bowed string instrument, a note in the harmonic series of a particular string can be played without the fundamental present.
One of a class of functions that enter into the development of the potential of a nearly spherical mass due to its attraction.
One's child.
ex: Games for the harmonics, (children), YL's and XYL's and the OM's, plus free soda for all.
The harmonics (kids, I mean) sometimes failed to recognize me on the rare occasions when I emerged from the shack […]

s.def: A function of two, three or n variables which is a solution to any of Laplace's equations

ety: From armonica. Coined by American polymath and statesman Benjamin Franklin to refer to his glass harmonica, an instrument that predated the small wind instrument by several decades. Doublet of harmonic; compare Latin harmonicus.

s.def: A musical wind instrument with a series of holes for the player to blow into, each hole producing a different note.
A musical instrument, consisting of a series of hemispherical glasses which, by touching the edges with the dampened finger, give forth the tones.
A toy instrument of strips of glass or metal hung on two tapes, and struck with hammers.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥-mo-n Ancient Greek *ἁρμων (*harmōn) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-i-eh₂ Proto-Hellenic *-íā Ancient Greek -ία (-ía) Ancient Greek ᾰ̔ρμονῐ́ᾱ (hărmonĭ́ā)bor. Latin harmoniabor. Italian armoniader. English armonica English harmonica Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Hellenic *-t…

s.def: someone who plays a harmonica
plural of harmonic
The science of musical sounds

ety: From Middle French harmonieux; by surface analysis, harmony + -ous.

s.def: Having components pleasingly or appropriately combined.
ex: The garden had a harmonious design, with flowers and shrubs complementing each other.

s.def: Showing accord in feeling or action.
ex: The team worked in a harmonious atmosphere, achieving great results.

s.def: Melodious; in harmony.
ex: The choir’s voices blended in a harmonious melody.

ety: From harmony + -ist. Compare French harmoniste.

s.def: One who shows the agreement of corresponding passages of different authors, as of the four Biblical evangelists.
One who understands the principles of harmony or is skillful in applying them in composition; a composer.

ety: Borrowed from French harmonium, coined by French harmonium inventor Alexandre Debain in 1840. By surface analysis, harmony + -ium. First attested in 1847.

s.def: A small keyboard instrument that consists of a series of reed pipes, which sound when one of the keys is pressed to open a valve that allows air to pass through.
ex: Pianos, melodiums, harmoniums, eolinas, &c. too dear at any price.
The only other man was a little grey-headed fellow with a pleasant face and quick, twinkling eyes, who sat at a harmonium in the corner.
They were a grave and reverend seignior in a frock coat, a lady sitting at a portable harmonium, and a chinless youth toying with a crucifix.

s.def: Synonym of Hooke's atom.

ety: From French harmoniser. By surface analysis, harmony + -ize.

s.def: To be in harmonious agreement.
ex: This explanation of the clan totem harmonizes with the supposed effect of killing one of the totem species.

s.def: To play or sing in harmony.
To provide parts to.
To bring things into harmony, or to make things compatible; to reconcile; juggle.
To provide the harmony for a melody.

ety: From Middle English armonye, from Old French harmonie, armonie, from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía, “joint, union, agreement, concord of sounds”), either from or cognate with ἁρμόζω (harmózō, “to fit together”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to join, fit, fix together”). First attested in 1602. Doublet of harmonia.

s.def: Agreement or accord.
A pleasing combination of elements, or arrangement of sounds.
The academic study of chords.
Two or more notes played simultaneously to produce a chord.
The relationship between two distinct musical pitches (musical pitches being frequencies of vibration which produce audible sound) played simultaneously.
A literary work which brings together or arranges systematically parallel passages of historians respecting the same events, and shows their agreement or consistency.
ex: a harmony of the Gospels

ety: From Middle English harneys, harnes, harneis, harnais, herneis, from Anglo-Norman harneis and Old French hernois (“equipment used in battle”), believed to be from Old Norse *hernest, from herr (“army”) + nest (“provisions”) (from Proto-Germanic *nesaną (“to heal, recover”)). More at harry.

s.def: A restraint or support, especially one consisting of a loop or network of rope or straps, and especially one worn by a working animal such as a horse pulling a carriage or farm implement.
A collection of wires or cables bundled and routed according to their function: a wiring harness.
The complete dress, especially in a military sense, of a man or a horse; armour in general.
ex: Ring the alarum-bell! Blow, wind! come, wrack! At least we'll die with harness on our back.
Under the sea-girt cliffs the shining ship was readied, laden with coats of mail, swords, and gleaming war harness.

s.def: The part of a loom comprising the heddles, with their means of support and motion, by which the threads of the warp are alternately raised and depressed for the passage of the shuttle.
Equipment for any kind of labour.
A software framework.
ex: test harness

s.def: To place a harness on something; to tie up or restrain.
ex: They harnessed the horse to the post.

s.def: To capture, control or put to use.
ex: Imagine what might happen if it were possible to harness solar energy fully.

s.def: To equip with armour.
The part of a harness which supports the weight of poles or shafts attaching a vehicle to a horse or other animal.

ety: From Middle English harpe, from Old English hearpe (“harp”), from Proto-West Germanic *harpā, from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ (“harp”). Cognate with Scots hairp (“harp”), West Frisian harpe, harp (“harp”), Low German Harp (“harp”), Dutch harp (“harp”), German Harfe (“harp”), Danish harpe (“harp”), Swedish harpa (“harp”).

s.def: A musical instrument consisting of a body and a curved neck, strung with strings of varying length that are stroked or plucked with the fingers and are vertical to the soundboard when viewed from the end of the body
Any musical instrument.
A grain sieve.
The component of a lamp to which one attaches the lampshade, consisting of a lightweight frame that usually surrounds the bulb with an attachment at the top for the finial.
ex: Both types of harp have a swiveling shade holder at the top. The threaded stud on the swivel accepts the finial.

s.def: Ellipsis of harp seal.
To repeatedly mention a subject, especially so as to nag or complain.
ex: Why do you harp on a single small mistake?
Why do you harp on about a single small mistake?

s.def: To play on (a harp or similar instrument).
To develop or give expression to by skill and art; to sound forth as from a harp; to hit upon.
To play (a tune) on the harp.
One of the moons of Jupiter.

ety: From Old French harpon, from Latin harpaga, a variant of Latin harpagō, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch away, to carry off, to seize, to captivate”). Sense and spelling perhaps influenced by Dutch harpoen (“harpoon”). Doublet of harpagon.

s.def: A spearlike weapon with a barbed head used in hunting whales and large fish.
A sharp tip within a disposable syringe, used to penetrate the stopper.
A harmonica.
ex: I took my harpoon out of my dirty red bandana.

s.def: To shoot something with a harpoon.
ex: Pilot whales, also known as blackfish, were fairly plentiful, and Mundus would harpoon one or two, haul them out onto the beach, and butcher them.

ety: From harpoon + -er.

s.def: A person who uses a harpoon, especially to hunt whales.
ex: Y.T. laughs. So does Raven. "What's your job?" Y.T. asks. "I'm a harpooner," he says.

ety: Early 1600s, borrowed from French harpechord (“harp string”), from New Latin harpichordium, from harpa (“harp”) + chorda (“string”). Influenced by and possibly also borrowed from Italian arpicordo, producing variant spellings. The unetymological -s-, which predominates by the 1660s, is of unclear origin.

s.def: A stringed musical instrument with a keyboard, the mechanical precusor to the fortepiano, in which each key causes a plectrum to pluck a corresponding tuned string, producing a bright, sharp tone similar to that of a harp.

ety: Ultimately from Middle French harpie, from Latin harpyia, from Ancient Greek ἅρπυιᾰ (hárpuiă, literally “snatcher”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch, seize”). Compare rapacious. Middle English had arpie.

s.def: A mythological creature generally depicted as a bird-of-prey with the head of a maiden, a face pale with hunger and long claws on her hands personifying the destructive power of storm winds.
ex: Both table and provisions vanish'd quite, With sound of harpies' wings and talons heard.

s.def: Any of a number of eagle-like birds of prey of the subfamily Harpiinae, especially the species Harpia harpyja.
The European moor buzzard or marsh harrier (Circus aeruginosus).
A shrewish woman.
ex: But her most subtle wiles proved ineffectual in ridding her, even for a moment, of her harpy jailer[…]

s.def: One who is rapacious or ravenous; an extortioner.
ex: c. 1772, Oliver Goldsmith, letter to Mrs. Bunbury The harpies about me all pocket the pool.

ety: From French harquebuse, borrowed from Middle Low German hakebusse or Middle Dutch hakebus, hagebus (modern Dutch haakbus), from hôk (“hook”) + busse (“box; firelock”), from Old Saxon hōk + *buhsa, from Proto-Germanic *hōkaz + *buhsā.

s.def: An obsolete matchlock firearm.
A portable gun, varying in size from a small cannon to a musket. When used in the field it was supported upon a tripod or trestle.

ety: Perhaps a modification of French haridelle (“old horse, nag”).

s.def: A vicious and scolding woman, especially an older one.
ex: Well there was one old lady, and a drunken old harridan she was surely, that paid all her attention to me.

ety: Etymology tree English harry Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English harrier From harry + -er.

s.def: One who harries.
Any of several birds of prey in the genus Circus of the subfamily Circinae which fly low over meadows and marshes and hunt small mammals or birds.
A runner, specifically, a cross country runner.
A kind of dog used to hunt hares; a harehound.

ety: From Middle English harwe, harow, from Old English *hearwa (perhaps ultimately cognate with harvest), or from Old Norse harfr/herfi; compare Danish harve (“harrow”), Dutch hark (“rake”). Akin to Latin carpere. According to the OED, the verb senses are partly derived from the noun sense, partly from a by-form of the verb harry, itself from Old English hergian.

s.def: A device consisting of a heavy framework having several disks or teeth in a row, which is dragged across ploughed land to smooth or break up the soil, to remove weeds or cover seeds; a harrow plow.
ex: Part of your job would be to learn tractor ploughing and the use of planters, harrows, and cultivators.

s.def: An obstacle formed by turning an ordinary harrow upside down, the frame being buried.
To drag a harrow over; to break up with a harrow.
To traumatize or disturb; to torment, distress or vex.
ex: It harrows me with fear and wonder.
The headless horseman harrowed Ichabod Crane as he tried to reach the bridge.

s.def: To break or tear, as if with a harrow; to wound; to lacerate.
ex: my aged muscles harrow'd up with whips

s.def: A call for help, or of distress, alarm etc.
ex: Harrow, the flames, which me consume (said hee) / Ne can be quencht, within my secret bowels bee.

ety: From Middle English herien, harien, from Old English herġian, from Proto-West Germanic *harjōn, from Proto-Germanic *harjōną, from *harjaz (“army”), from Proto-Indo-European *koryos, from *ker- (“army”). Cognates See also Walloon hairyî, Old French hairier, harier; also Saterland Frisian ferheerje, German verheeren (“to harry, devastate”), Swedish härja (“ravage, harry”); also Old English here, West Frisian hear, Dutch heer, German Heer); also Middle Irish cuire (“army”), Lithuanian kãrias (“ar…

s.def: To plunder, pillage, assault.
ex: I repent me much , That so I harry'd him

s.def: To make repeated attacks on an enemy.
To strip, lay waste, ravage.
ex: to harry this beautiful region
A red squirrel had harried the nest of a wood thrush.

s.def: To harass, bother or distress with demands, threats, or criticism.
ex: Chelsea also struggled to keep possession as QPR harried and chased at every opportunity, giving their opponents no time on the ball.

s.def: A menial servant; a sweeper.

ety: From Middle English harsk, harisk(e), hask(e), herris. Century derived the term from Old Norse harskr (whence Danish harsk (“rancid”), dialectal Norwegian hersk, Swedish härsk, Swedish härsken); the Middle English Dictionary derives it from that and Middle Low German harsch (“rough”, literally “hairy”) (whence also German harsch), from haer (“hair”), from Old Saxon hār, from Proto-West Germanic *hār; the Oxford Dictionary of English derives it from Middle Low German alone.

s.def: Unpleasantly rough to the touch or other senses.
Severe or cruel.
ex: harsh decision
harsh penalty
harsh teacher

s.def: To negatively criticize.
ex: Quit harshing me already, I said that I was sorry!
Stop harshing on yourself. Who said you're the ugly sister?
“Stop harshing on me, Daddy.” “Harshing?” “Don't yell at me. I didn't do anything.”

s.def: To put a damper on (a mood).
ex: Dude, you're harshing my buzz.
They're always harshing on the plan, but we're still going through with it.
"They're mostly mercenaries these days. But whose?" "Serbian mercenaries? You're harshing my groove, man. I'm gonna pretend I didn't hear that...."

ety: From Middle English harsknes; equivalent to harsh + -ness.

s.def: The quality of being harsh.

ety: From Middle English hert, from Old English heorot (“stag”), from Proto-West Germanic *herut, from Proto-Germanic *herutaz (compare Dutch hert, German Hirsch, Danish/Norwegian/Swedish hjort), from Pre-Germanic *kerudos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“horn”). Doublet of Heorot. Cognates Compare Welsh carw (“deer”), Latin cervus (“deer”), cervīx (“nape of the neck”), Lithuanian kárvė (“cow”), Russian коро́ва (koróva, “cow”), Ancient Greek κόρυδος (kórudos, “crested lark”), κορυφή (koruphḗ, “su…

s.def: A male deer, especially the male of the red deer after his fifth year.
The meat from this animal.
ex: We are to have hart for dinner on Jack’s birthday; you call it deer in Grenada.
The people of Israel knew something of hunting, as in the stories of eating hart and roebuck, and venison.
Still, the people of Israel certainly knew about hunting, because they ate hart (red deer) and roe deer.

s.def: The stag of any deer species.
Obsolete spelling of heart.

ety: From Hector (“in Greek and Roman mythology, a character in Homer’s Iliad who is the greatest warrior of Troy”), from Late Middle English Hector (“warrior with the qualities of Hector”), from Latin Hectōr or Ancient Greek Ἕκτωρ (Héktōr), from ἕκτωρ (héktōr, “holding fast”), from ἔχειν (ékhein), present active infinitive of ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, own, possess; to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“to hold; to overpower”). The verb is derived from the noun.

s.def: Sometimes in the form Hector: a blustering, noisy, turbulent fellow; a braggart, bully.
To dominate or intimidate in a blustering way; to bully, to domineer.
To behave like a hector or bully; to bluster, to swagger; to bully.
ex: Leave me alone! Will you leave me alone! Hectored by women all my life—hectored by women—first one, then another. I won't stand it—I won't stand it—

rel: Not to be confused with hectare

ety: From Latin Hectōr or Ancient Greek Ἕκτωρ (Héktōr), from ἕκτωρ (héktōr, “holding fast”), from ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“to hold; to overpower”). Sometimes used as an anglicization of various Scottish Gaelic names, including Eachann and Eochaid. The thundercloud cluster was named by pilots during the Second World War.

s.def: A Trojan hero in Homer's Iliad.
A male given name from Ancient Greek.
A place name:
A thundercloud cluster that forms nearly every afternoon from approximately September to March near the Tiwi Islands of Australia, reaching a height and width of 20 kilometers.

ety: Deliberately altered spelling of head, to distinguish the word as not belonging in a journalistic story. Compare lede (“lead, introduction”). Also an archaic spelling.

s.def: The headline of a news story.
Archaic spelling of head.
Pronunciation spelling of had, representing dialectal English.
ex: ‘An’ th’ dumblasted rascal hed to go an’ git gay wi’ June. Dick turned to an’ hammered seven hells out o’ his mug an’ hove him out on deck—’

s.def: simple past and past participle of heed
ex: They finally hed my warnings!

ety: From Middle English helde, from Old English hefeld, from the root of Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to have, heave”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Cognate with Old Saxon hevild, Middle Low German hevelte, Icelandic hafald.

s.def: A component in a loom, being one of a number of similar components, through the eye of each of which a distinct strand of the warp is threaded.
ex: The heddles and heddle frames, Fig. 3, and the reed may be purchased from dealers in craftwork supplies.

s.def: One of the sets of parallel doubled threads which, with mounting, compose the harness employed to guide the warp threads to the lathe or batten in a loom.
To thread each strand of the warp through the eye of a heddle.
ex: After each frame has been heddled, stand upright within easy reach until the full set has been completed.

ety: From Middle English hegge, from Old English heċġ, from Proto-West Germanic *haggju, from Proto-Germanic *hagjō, from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰyóm (“enclosure”). Cognate with Dutch heg, German Hecke. Doublet of hey (a choreographic figure) and quay. More at haw.

s.def: A thicket of bushes or other shrubbery, especially one planted as a fence between two portions of land, or to separate the parts of a garden.
ex: He trims the hedge once a week.

s.def: A barrier (often consisting of a line of persons or objects) to protect someone or something from harm.
A mound of earth, stone- or turf-faced, often topped with bushes, used as a fence between any two portions of land.
A noncommittal or intentionally ambiguous statement.
Contract or arrangement reducing one's exposure to risk (for example the risk of price movements or interest rate movements).
ex: The asset class acts as a hedge.

s.def: With indication of a person's upbringing, or professional activities, taking place by the side of the road; being third-rate, poor, shoddy.
ex: He then traced them from place to place, till at last he found two of them drinking together, with a third person, at a hedge-tavern near Aldersgate.
This particular wheelwright is only a hedge carpenter, without even a shop of his own,[…].

s.def: To enclose with a hedge or hedges.
ex: to hedge a field or garden

s.def: To obstruct or surround.
ex: Lollius Urbius […] drew another wall […] to hedge out incursions from the north.

s.def: To offset the risk associated with.
To avoid verbal commitment.
ex: He carefully hedged his statements with weasel words.

ety: From Middle English heyghoge; equivalent to hedge + hog. Eclipsed non-native Middle English yrchoun, irchoun (“hedgehog”), from Old French hirchoun, herichon (“hedgehog”); and displaced earlier Middle English il, from Old English īl, iġil (“hedgehog”). In the philosophical sense, from the 1953 essay The Hedgehog and the Fox by Isaiah Berlin. Compare typologically Korean 고슴도치 (goseumdochi) (<<+ Middle Korean 돝 (twoth, “pig, swine”)).

s.def: animal
A small mammal of the subfamily Erinaceinae, characterized by their spiny back and often by the habit of rolling up into a ball when attacked, native to Afro-Eurasia.
ex: Among the Romans the genital organ of the hedgehog and the wolf were among the ingredients used in aphrodisiac concoctions.

s.def: Any of several spiny mammals, such as the porcupine, that are similar to the hedgehog.
Ellipsis of Czech hedgehog (“an antitank obstacle constructed from three steel rails”).

A spigot mortar-type of depth charge weapon from World War II that simultaneously fires a number of explosives into the water to create a pattern of underwater explosions intended to attack submerged submarines.
A type of chocolate cake (or slice), somewhat similar to an American brownie.
ex: I am so flustered that I order a vanilla slice instead of hedgehog.
His wife had made a hedgehog cake and he offered some but Murphy refused – his mouth was so dry with terror he couldn′t swallow.

s.def: A form of dredging machine.
Certain flowering plants with parts resembling a member of family Erinaceidae
The edible fungus Hydnum repandum.
ex: Hedgehogs fruit from autumn until late spring. Many consumers are still unfamiliar with hedgehogs, and they have a relatively small commercial trade.

s.def: A kind of electrical transformer with open magnetic circuit, the ends of the iron wire core being turned outward and presenting a bristling appearance.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂d-der. English -ism English hedonism From Ancient Greek ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”) + English -ism. First attested in 1856.

s.def: The philosophical belief that prioritizes happiness, particularly sensual pleasure as the highest good in life.
A general devotion to the pursuit of pleasure.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂d-der. s.def: Someone devoted to hedonism.

ety: Onomatopoeic coinage.

s.def: The cry of an ass or donkey.
Alternative form of heebie-jeebies.

ety: From Middle English heden, from Old English hēdan (“to heed, take care, observe, attend, guard, take charge, take possession, receive”), from Proto-West Germanic *hōdijan (“to heed, guard”), from Proto-Indo-European *kadʰ- (“to heed, protect”). Cognate with West Frisian hoedje (“to heed”), Dutch hoeden (“to heed”), German hüten (“to heed”).

s.def: Careful attention.
To guard, protect.
To mind; to regard with care; to take notice of; to attend to; to observe.
ex: With pleasure Argus the musician heeds.
"It comes back to me that I wanted to say something to the driver and that I couldn't make him heed me."
The help tended to be officious, the rules, if heeded, restrictive, and the management meddlesome.

s.def: To pay attention, care.

ety: From heed + -ful.

s.def: Taking heed.
Paying close attention; mindful.

ety: Etymology tree English heed Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *lewHs-der. Proto-Germanic *leusaną Proto-Germanic *lausaz Proto-Germanic *-lausaz Proto-West Germanic *-laus Old English -lēas Middle English -les English -less English heedless From heed + -less.

s.def: Unaware; without noticing; careless; inattentive.
ex: Sing we joyous, all together, heedless of the wind and weather.

s.def: Alternative spelling of hee-haw.
Alternative spelling of hee-haw.
Alternative spelling of hee-haw.

ety: From Middle English hele, from Old English hēla, from Proto-West Germanic *hą̄hilō, from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *hanhaz (“heel, hock”), equivalent to hock + -le. More at hock. Compare North Frisian haiel, West Frisian hyl, Dutch hiel, German Low German Hiel, Danish and Norwegian hæl, Swedish häl.

s.def: The rear part of the foot, where it joins the leg.
ex: He [the stag] calls to mind his strength and then his speed, / His winged heels and then his armed head.

s.def: The part of a shoe's sole which supports the foot's heel.
The rear part of a sock or similar covering for the foot.
The part of the palm of a hand closest to the wrist.
ex: He drove the heel of his hand into the man's nose.

s.def: A high-heeled shoe.
ex: She'd been wearing heels, and fell backward off her right heel and twisted or broke her ankle.

Oh mama, I'm just having fun On the stage in my heels It's where I belong down at the...

s.def: The back, upper part of the stock.
The thickening of the neck of a stringed instrument where it attaches to the body.
The last or lowest part of anything.
ex: the heel of a mast
the heel of a vessel

s.def: A crust end-piece of a loaf of bread.
ex: the heel of the white loaf
Boiled mutton was in one, and the heel of a damper in another.
`Have ye seen,' said Uncle Jobson with basilisk severity, `what's become of the heel of to-day's loaf?'

s.def: The base of a bun sliced in half lengthwise.
ex: The bottom half, or the bun heel is placed in the carton, and the pickle slices spread evenly over the meat or cheese.

s.def: The large bone making up the heel of the human foot.

ety: Etymology tree Middle English hele English heel English -er English heeler From heel + -er.

s.def: A gamecock that strikes well with its heels or spurs.
A quick runner.
ex: That a crowd of Sydney stealers, Jockeys, pugilists and spielers Brought some horses, real heelers, Came and put us through.

s.def: A dog that readily comes to heel.
ex: If your dog is a good heeler, you'll find some competition in the obedience ring.

s.def: A dog used for cattle droving.
A dependent and subservient hanger-on of a political patron.
ex: The army of hungry heelers who do their bidding.

s.def: The rodeo performer who ropes the steer by its hind feet after the header has turned it.
A student journalist at Yale University.

ety: From heel + tap.

s.def: A piece or wedge that raises the heel of a shoe.
A small amount of (especially alcoholic) drink remaining at the bottom of a glass.
ex: "He's a good fellow, anyway, if he is a teetotaler!" "Drink his health!" "Give him a rouser, and no heeltaps!"
We had the heeltaps of bottles as well, so that we often drank too much—a good thing, for one seemed to work faster when partially drunk.

s.def: To add a piece of leather to the heel of (a shoe, boot, etc.).

ety: The noun is derived from Late Middle English heft (“heaviness; something heavy, a weight”), from heven (“to lift, raise”) + -th (suffix denoting a condition, quality, state of being, etc., forming nouns), by analogy with the development of weft from weven (modern English weave), etc. (also compare words like cleft from cleave, and theft from thieve, where the development occurred in Old English or earlier languages). The English word is analysable as heave + -t (suffix forming nouns from verbs)…

s.def: The feel of the weight of something; heaviness.
ex: A high quality hammer should have good balance and heft.
I pictured him doing violence to his better nature, and only wanting a good heft of circumstance to enable him to throw off his load of deviltry.
Unlike most moons of the solar system, ours has the heft to pull itself into a sphere.

s.def: The force exerted by an object due to gravitation; weight.
ex: "Look at the heft of 'n [a baby]," said the proud father, "entirely drags ye down, Miss Sybil, 'e do."

s.def: Graveness, seriousness; gravity.
ex: He's got a good voice, and reads well; but come to a sermon—wal, ain't no gret heft in't.

s.def: Importance, influence; weight.
The greater part of something; the bulk, the mass.
ex: The turkey's nest was islanded with a fragrant swath,—the "heft" of the crop noted and rejoiced over,—[…]
He run to South America or somewheres, taking the heft of the firm's money with him.

s.def: An act of lifting; a lift.

s.def: An act of heaving (lifting with difficulty); an instance of violent exertion or straining.
ex: The socket of the rim lock tore off to one good heft of the shoulder, and we were in.

s.def: To lift or lift up (something, especially a heavy object).
ex: He hefted the sack of concrete into the truck.
[…] Bevis was to "heft" his gun to the shoulder, and only to press it there sufficiently to feel that the butt touched him.
[H]e found that he was hefting the bench leg, curiously, as though trying its balance, as if he had never touched it before.

s.def: To test the weight of (something) by lifting.
ex: Sim's ben to college, and he's putty smart and chipper. Come to heft him, tho', he don't weigh much 'longside o' Parson Cushing.

s.def: To have (substantial) weight; to weigh.

ety: 19th century. From heft (“weight”) + -y. The similarity with German heftig (“vigorous, violent, intense”) is apparently coincidental. From the German are Dutch, Danish, Norwegian heftig, Swedish häftig.

s.def: With heft; heavy, strong, vigorous, mighty, impressive
ex: He can throw a hefty punch.
The Remove dormitory echoed to the old, familiar sound of Bunter's hefty snore.

s.def: Strong; bulky.
ex: They use some hefty bolts to hold up road signs.

s.def: Possessing physical strength and weight; rugged and powerful; powerfully or heavily built.
ex: He was a tall, hefty man.

s.def: Heavy, weighing a lot.
ex: She carries a hefty backpack full of books.

s.def: Large, healthy.
ex: That's going to cost you a hefty sum.
a hefty fine

ety: From Ancient Greek ἡγεμονία (hēgemonía, “supremacy or leadership, chief command”), from ἡγεμών (hēgemṓn, “a leader, guide, commander, chief”), from ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead”). Early 19th-century usage influenced by German Hegemonie.

s.def: Domination, influence, or authority over another, especially by one political group over a society or by one nation over others.
ex: The idea of a German republic and confederacy like the American, is surely less fantastical than a hegemony to which nobody is willing to submit.

s.def: Dominance of one social group over another, such that the ruling group or hegemon acquires some degree of consent from the subordinate, as opposed to dominance purely by force.
ex: The two political parties battled viciously for hegemony.

ety: From Arabic هِجْرَة (hijra, “exodus; emigration”). Doublet of hijra.

s.def: A journey taken to escape from danger; an exodus.
ex: By all odds the most remarkable westward migration before the California gold rush of 1849 was the Mormon hegira to the Great Salt Lake basin.

ety: From Middle English hehe, from Old English he he.

s.def: An approximation to the sound of a mischievous giggle.
ex: And then his trousers fell down, hehe.

ety: Inherited from Middle English heyfre, hayfre, heyfer, from Old English hēahfore, hēahfru, of disputed origin; see the Old English entry for more discussion.

s.def: A young female cow, (particularly) one over one year old but which has not calved.
ex: And when the lorries unload their cows / Their hogs, their heifers and sows / In piles of slithering meat

s.def: An unattractive or unpleasant woman.
ex: I have half a mind to marry that heifer, tho' wives are bothersome critters when you have too many of them.
Stop your crying, heifer, I don't need all that, I got a job for you, the braided-up pimp is back!
My hand was aching to slap that silly heifer. I told her to take her trifling ass down to Burger King and get herself a job flipping burgers...

s.def: A wife.
ex: Her, whom I shall choose for my heicfar.

ety: Inherited from Middle English heigh, hey, hay, hei, heh, probably of imitative origin. Compare hey, eh.

s.def: An exclamation designed to call attention, give encouragement, etc.
ex: Heigh, my hearts! Cheerly, cheerly, my hearts.

The distance of something above the ground or some other chosen level.
ex: We flew at a height of 15 000 meters.
I'm afraid of heights.

s.def: A quality of vowels, indicating the vertical position of the tongue relative to the roof of the mouth; in practice, the first formant, associated with the height of the tongue.

ety: From Middle English heightenen, hyghtenen, equivalent to height + -en (verbal suffix).

s.def: To make high; to raise higher; to elevate.
ex: Black Bridge, near Machynlleth, is being heightened by one metre in a £3.6 million project to reduce delays caused by flooding.

s.def: To advance, increase, augment, make larger, more intense, stronger etc.
ex: to heighten beauty
to heighten a flavor or a tint
to heighten awareness

A Sieg Heil.

ety: From Middle English heynous, from Anglo-Norman hainous, heinous (compare French haineux) from Old French haïr, hadir (“to hate”) (compare Old French en-hadir (“to become filled with hate”)), from Frankish *hattjan (“to hate”) (compare Middle English hetien). s.def: Totally reprehensible.
ex: I hope they catch the person responsible for that heinous crime.
The perpetrators of this heinous act must be brought to justice.

s.def: Bad, evil or villainous.

ety: From Middle English heir, from Anglo-Norman eir, heir, from Latin hērēs.

s.def: Someone who inherits, or is designated to inherit, the property of another.
ex: My brother is the heir to our childhood house and yet has no interest in it.
I am my father's heir and only son.

s.def: One who inherits, or has been designated to inherit, a hereditary title or office.
ex: As the heir to the British throne, the Prince of Wales is a very public figure.

s.def: A successor in a role, representing continuity with the predecessor.
ex: And I his heir in misery alone.

Sergeant Schlock has no horse, no armor, and no sword, but even the mightiest Mongol horse-warrior would see in him a fit heir.

ety: From heir + -dom.

s.def: An inheritance or succession.

A woman who has received an inheritance.

ety: From heir + -ship.

ex: He began to fear lest he should be obliged to fulfil the duty of heirship to the property deposited with him.

A fiction genre in which a heist is central to the plot; a work in such a genre.

The crew resemble typical heist characters[.]

ety: From Old Norse hel. Cognate with Old English hell (“hell”).

The goddess of the realm of the unheroic dead, a daughter of Loki by the jotun Angrboða.
The realm of the dead who did not die in combat, ruled by the goddess and located in Niflheim (one of the Nine Realms).

A dragonfly; so named due to its resemblance to a helicopter (sense 1).
A whirling trick performed with devil sticks.
A breakdance move in which the dancer spins on the floor while extending the legs to resemble the blades of a helicopter.

ety: From Middle English herbage, from Old French erbage, from Early Medieval Latin herbāticum, from Latin herba (“grass”). By surface analysis, herb + -age.

s.def: Herbs collectively.
Herbaceous plant growth, especially grass.
ex: I threw myself upon my face, and clung to the scant herbage in an excess of nervous agitation.
The dank breath of herbage, sodden with rain, came to her; the mists were barely visible, hovering above the dark ravines.

s.def: The fleshy, often edible, parts of plants.
The natural pasture of a land, considered as distinct from the land itself; hence, right of pasture (on another man's land).

ety: Borrowed from Old French herbal. By surface analysis, herb + -al

s.def: Made from or with herbs.
ex: Herbal tea has a nice aroma and is good for a stuffy head.

s.def: Made from natural herbs specifically as opposed to from synthetic materials.
ex: a herbal remedy for back-ache

s.def: A manual of herbs and their medical uses.
ex: It can still be found in herbals and such, which describe it as a sedative and cough suppressant.

s.def: An herbal supplement.
ex: I took a ride to the shopping strip at Belmont and Central and stocked up on herbals at three Polish New Age health stores.

s.def: A beverage made by infusing mainly the leaves (and sometimes the flowers, roots, or stems) of various herbs or other plants, generally not including true tea (Camellia sinensis).

ety: Etymology tree English herbal Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Hellenic *-tās Ancient Greek -τής (-tḗs) Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs)bor. ety: From Latin herbārium. Doublet of arbor.

s.def: A substance used to kill plants.

ety: Adapted borrowing of New Latin herbivorus + -ous, from Latin herba (“grass”) and -vorus, from vorō (“to devour”).

s.def: Feeding chiefly on plants.
ex: One example of "an herbivorous fungus" is included among the terrestrial animal experiments

s.def: A town and municipality of Montenegro.
Alternative letter-case form of Herculean.
ex: Similarly, Joseph E. May, M.D., prescribed herculean doses of calomel and quinine to a slave with malaria, who, fortunately, recovered.

ety: From Latin Herculēs, from Etruscan 𐌇𐌄𐌓𐌂𐌋𐌄 (hercle), from Ancient Greek Ἡρακλῆς (Hēraklês), apparently cognate of Ἥρα (Hḗra, “Hera”) and, according to Haudry, from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”) + κλέος (kléos, “glory”). Doublet of Heracles.

s.def: The Roman name for the Greek divine hero Heracles, who was the son of Jupiter and Alcmene, a celebrated hero who possessed exceptional strength. Most famous for his twelve labours performed to redeem himself after killing his family.
ex: […]—Hercules—Was Nimrod, the grand-son of Noah, and the origin of all the fabled Herculesses of all the early nations—[…]
Our great cities have become so many Augean stables, for the removal of whose filth as many Hercules are required.

s.def: A summer constellation of the northern sky, said to resemble the mythical hero, lying between the constellations Lyra and Corona Borealis.
A crater in the first quadrant on the moon.
A male given name from Ancient Greek.
A city in Contra Costa County, California, United States.

ety: From Middle English herde, heerde, heorde, from Old English hierd, heord (“herd, flock; keeping, care, custody”), from Proto-West Germanic *herdu, from Proto-Germanic *herdō (“herd”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerdʰ- (“file, row, herd”). Cognate with German Herde, Danish hjord, Swedish hjord. Non-Germanic cognates include Albanian herdhe (“nest”) and Serbo-Croatian krdo.

s.def: A number of domestic animals assembled together under the watch or ownership of a keeper.
ex: a herd of cattle
a herd of sheep
a herd of goats

s.def: Any collection of animals gathered or travelling in a company.
ex: Zakouma is the last place on Earth where you can see more than a thousand elephants on the move in a single, compact herd.
Zebras can also be called a herd or a zeal.

s.def: To manage, care for or guard a herd
ex: He is employed to herd the goats.

s.def: A crowd, a mass of people or things; a rabble.
ex: I was never one to follow the herd.
You can never interest the common herd in the abstract question.

s.def: A collection of things, especially vehicles.
ex: Herds of buses spread across the streets.

s.def: To unite or associate in a herd; to feed or run together, or in company.
ex: Sheep herd on many hills.
Any predator that preys on animals that herd or school, has to be able to single out one individual to attack.

s.def: To unite or associate in a herd
To associate; to ally oneself with, or place oneself among, a group or company.
To move, or be moved, in a group. (of both animals and people)
ex: On alighting at the station, we were all herded over the footbridge and through a side exit.

s.def: Someone who keeps a group of domestic animals.
ex: Near-synonym: herdsman
John Dodds, the herd who bode in the place, was standing at the door, and he looked to see who was on the road so late.

ety: From herd + immunity, first identified in herds of cattle.

s.def: The indirect protection against the spread of a contagious disease in a given population caused by the immunity of a significant proportion of the population to that particular disease; the immunity may have been obtained through having survived the infection or through vaccination.
ex: For herd immunity to occur, the vaccine must prevent transmission of the virus as well as prevent disease.

ety: From Middle English herder, herdere, hurder (attested as a surname), an alteration of Middle English herde (“herder, herdsman”), from Old English hyrde, hierde (“herder”), from Proto-West Germanic *hirdī, from Proto-Germanic *hirdijaz, equivalent to herd + -er. Doublet of herd ("herder"), as in cowherd, goatherd, shepherd, etc.

s.def: One who herds.
ex: Near-synonym: herdsman

s.def: A dog, such as the various shepherd breeds, that are bred for working cattle, sheep, or other livestock.

ety: From herd + -s- + -man.

s.def: A person who tends livestock, especially cows and sheep; especially, the foreman among a group of such farmworkers, usually with more knowledge and experience.

ety: From Middle English her, from Old English hēr (“at this place”), from Proto-West Germanic *hēr, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r, from *hiz + *-r, from Proto-Indo-European *kís, from *ḱe + *ís. Cognates Cognate with Saterland Frisian hier, West Frisian hjir, Dutch hier, German Low German hier, German hier, Danish her, Swedish här, Norwegian her, Faroese her, Icelandic hér. Also related to the English pronoun he (“this/that person”), and the words hither (“to this place”) and hence (“from this place”).

s.def: In, on, or at this place (a place perceived to be close to the speaker); compare there.
ex: You wait here while I fetch my coat.
Ms. Doe is not here at the moment.
It says here that he died in 1970.

s.def: To this place; used in place of the literary or archaic hither.
ex: Please come here.

s.def: Alive

ex: Here is where I met my spouse twelve years ago.

s.def: This time, the present situation.
Used semi-assertively to offer something to the listener.
ex: Here, now I'm giving it to you.

s.def: Used for emphasis at the beginning of a sentence when expressing an opinion or want.
ex: Here, I'm tired and I want a drink.

s.def: Used to attract someone's attention, often in a hostile way.
ex: Here! You! Stop doing that!

s.def: Said in response to one's name being called during a roll call, indicating that one is present.
ex: Smith ... Here! ... Jones ... Here! ... Walters ... ... Anyone seen Walters?

From time to time; intermittently, occasionally.

s.def: Said when handing something over to someone or doing a favour to them, usually to draw the recipient's attention to the exchange; equivalent to “thank you” when receiving something.
Used to express disdain for someone's actions despite the speaker's hopes or expectations.

ety: From hereabout + -s (See adverbial genitive).

s.def: Near here.
ex: The people hereabouts, sir, would seem to dispense with street illumination, and it is very dark tonight.

Hereabouts is Knockupworth, where the line deviates from the canal course.

ety: From Old English hēræfter (“in the aftertime; later on”). By surface analysis, here + after.

s.def: In time to come; in some future time or state.

[…] when hereafter he from war shall come / And bring his Trojans peace and triumph […]

Sequentially after this point (in time, in the writing constituting a document, in the movement along a path, etc.)
A future existence or state.
Existence after death.
ex: 'Tis the Divinity that stirs within us; / 'Tis Heaven itself that points out an hereafter, / and intimates eternity to man.

s.def: Future.

ety: From here + by.

ex: There is a mighty man, which wonnes hereby, / That with most fell despight and deadly hate / Seekes to subvert her Crowne and dignity […].

s.def: By this means, action or process.
ex: I hereby declare you husband and wife.

s.def: Capable of being inherited.
ex: Any Protestant who became a Catholic forfeited his whole hereditable estate to the nearest Protestant heir.

ety: Inherited from Middle English hereditarie, from Latin hērēditārius, from hērēditās (“inheritance”), from hērēs (“heir”).

ety: From Middle French heredité, from Latin hērēditas (“condition of being an heir”), from hēres (“heir”).

ex: laws of heredity
genetics and heredity
influence of heredity

ety: From Middle English here-inne, her-in, her-inne, hier-ine, from Old English hērinne, from Proto-West Germanic *hērinna, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂rinna, equivalent to here + in. Cognate with West Frisian hjiryn (“herein”), Dutch hierin (“herein”), German hierin (“herein”), Danish heri (“herein”), Swedish häri (“herein”), Icelandic hér í (“herein”).

ety: From Middle English heresie (Middle English her(esie) + -esy), from Old French heresie (modern hérésie), from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “choice, system of principles”), from αἱρέομαι (hairéomai, “to take for oneself, to choose”), the middle voice of αἱρέω (hairéō, “to take”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ser-; see also Welsh herw (“theft, raid”), Ancient Greek στερέω (steréō, “to deprive of”). Displaced native Old English dwild.

A controversial or unorthodox opinion held by a member of a group, as in politics, philosophy or science.

ety: From Middle English heretyk, heretike, from Old French eretique, from Medieval Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose, factious”), itself from Ancient Greek αἱρέω (hairéō, “to choose”).

ety: From Middle English heritage, from Old French eritage, heritage (modern French héritage), ultimately derived (through suffixation) from Latin hērēs. By surface analysis, herit + -age.

ety: From Middle English heriter, from Anglo-Norman heriter, Old French heritier, earlier eretier, eritier, from Late Latin hērēditārium (from the adjective hērēditārius (“hereditary”)), which took the place of hērēs (“heir”). ety: From Hermaphroditus, the mythical son of Hermes and Aphrodite, who merged bodies with a naiad, thereafter having both male and female qualities.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἑρμηνευτῐκός (hermēneutĭkós, “of or for interpreting”), from ἑρμηνεύω (hermēneúō, “translate, interpret”), from ἑρμηνεύς (hermēneús, “translator, interpreter”); sometimes ascribed as a Carian loanword. ety: From Middle English hermytage, ermitage, from Old French ermitage, hermitaige, from Latin erēmīta, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs, “hermit”). By surface analysis, hermit + -age.

ety: From Middle English heroes, from Old French heroes, from Latin hērōs (“hero”), from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs, “demi-god, hero”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to watch over, protect”); if so, related to Latin servo (“protect”). ety: From Middle English hien, hyen, highen, heiȝen, hiȝen, from Old English hīgian (“to hie, hasten, strive”), from Proto-West Germanic *hīgōn, from Proto-Germanic *hīgōną (“to breathe, snort”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱēygʰ- (“swift, fierce, violent”). ety: From hierarchy + -ical; compare French hiérarchique.

ety: From Middle English ierarchie, jerarchie, from Old French ierarchie, jerarchie, from Late Latin ierarchia, from Latin hierarchia, from Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία (hierarkhía, “rule of a high priest”), from ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs, “high priest”), from ἱερός (hierós, “holy”) + ἄρχω (árkhō, “to rule”), equivalent to hiero- + -archy. ety: From Latin hieraticus, from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós), from ἱερατεία (hierateía, “priesthood”), from ἱερατεύω (hierateúō, “be a priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”). s.def: Of or pertaining to priests or other religious authorities, especially pharaonic priests of Ancient Egypt.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἱερόδουλος (hieródoulos), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”) + δοῦλος (doûlos, “slave”).

ety: First attested around 1598, a back-formation from hieroglyphic (1580s), from Middle French hiéroglyphique, from Late Latin hieroglyphicus, from Ancient Greek ἱερογλυφικός (hierogluphikós) (Plutarch τά ἱερογλυφικά [γράμματα] "hieroglyphic [writing]), ἱερόγλυφος (hierógluphos, “carver of hieroglyphs”) (Ptolemy), a compound of ἱερός (hierós, “sacred, holy”) and γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carved work”), a calque of Egyptian mdw-nṯr (“the god’s word”), nTr-md. ety: From Middle English hirlyng, from Old English hȳrling (“hireling, employee”), from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀijuling. Cognate with West Frisian hierling, Dutch huurling (“hireling, mercenary”), German Low German Hüürling, German Heuerling. By surface analysis, hire + -ling.

s.def: An employee who is hired, often to perform unpleasant tasks with little independence.
ex: When my poor James was in the small-pox, did I allow any hireling to nurse him?

s.def: Someone who does a job purely for money, rather than out of interest in the work itself.
ex: These vain bickerings / Are spawn'd in courts by base intrigues and baser / Hirelings, who live by lies on good men's lives.

s.def: A horse for hire.
ex: In the afternoon they went to a neighbouring livery stables to look for hirellings.

s.def: A prostitute.

ety: Borrowed from Japanese 広(ひろ)島(しま) (Hiroshima). Transliteration of Japanese ひろしま

s.def: a city in Honshu, Japan
A prefecture in southwestern Honshu, Japan.
The capital city of Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan; the target of the first atomic bomb dropped in warfare on August 6, 1945.
ex: A short time ago, an American airplane dropped one bomb on Hiroshima and destroyed its usefulness to the enemy.

s.def: The 1945 atomic bombing of the city.
ex: VINCENT: Tens of thousands killed before sundown; nobody's killed people that fast since Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

ety: From Latin hirsūtus (“shaggy, hairy”).

s.def: Covered in hair or bristles; hairy.
ex: […] there are of Roots, Bulbous Roots, Fibrous Roots, and Hirsute Roots.
At that period, too, the Jew's long beard was far more distinctive than it is in this hirsute generation.
Ears small, with large lobes, indicating some Jewish blood. Hands small, well-tended, hirsute. Feet small.

s.def: Someone or something that is hirsute.
ex: Where’s the sockless hirsutes from the grasshopper-bitten wilds of Kansas?

ety: From Middle English hes, from Old English his (“his; its”), from Proto-Germanic *hes (“of this”), genitive of Proto-Germanic *hiz (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe-, *ḱey- (“this”). Cognate with Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, Icelandic hans (“his”). More at he; see also its.

s.def: Belonging to him.
Belonging to a person of unspecified gender.
Its; belonging to it. (Now only when implying personification.)
Used as a genitive marker in place of ’s after a noun, especially a masculine noun ending in -s, to express the possessive case.
ex: Ahab his mark
Sejanus his Fall

s.def: That or those belonging to him; the possessive case of he, used without a following noun.
ex: This pen is his. These books are also his.
The decision was his to live with.
His is bigger than mine.

s.def: His house or home.
ex: After our night out, I went back to his.

s.def: Alternative spelling of His.
plural of hi
ex: The Hikkams pushed a table over by the booth where the Lochwoods and Meekums were sitting, exchanged his and sat down.

ety: From Latin hispidus (“rough, hairy, bristly”).

s.def: Covered in short, stiff hairs.
ex: The hispid hare inhabits forested areas.

ety: From Middle English hissen, probably of onomatopoeic origin (compare Arabic هَسْهَسَ (hashasa)). Compare Middle Dutch hissen, hisschen (“to chase away, shoo”), Middle Low German hissen (“to chase, hound, incite”).

s.def: A sibilant sound, such as that made by a snake or escaping steam; an unvoiced fricative.
ex: Their music frightful as the serpent’s hiss, And boding screech-owls make the concert full!
[…] over head the dismal hiss Of fiery Darts in flaming volies flew,
[…] his form was soon covered over by the twilight as his footsteps mixed in with the low hiss of the leafy trees.

s.def: An expression of disapproval made using such a sound.
ex: […] in open disputations ye haue bene openly conuict, ye haue bene openly driuen out of the schole with hisses […]

s.def: To move with a hissing sound.
ex: The arrow hissed through the air.
The Troops of Troy recede with sudden Fear, While the swift Javelin hiss’d along in Air.
All shod with steel We hissed along the polished ice […]

s.def: To make a hiss, a sibilant sound of air escaping.
ex: As I started to poke it, the snake hissed at me.
The poor cat hissed as it backed away from the approaching man.
The frying pan hissed and sizzled as Ishvar gently slid ping-pong sized balls into the glistening oil.

s.def: To call someone by hissing.
To condemn or express contempt (for someone or something) by hissing.
ex: The crowd booed and hissed her off the stage.
The Play, perhaps, has many things amiss: Well, let us then reduce the point to this, Let only those that have no failings, hiss.
As the culprits went through the town and plantations they were laughed at, hissed, and hooted by the slaves […]

s.def: To utter (something) with a hissing sound.
ex: Lies oft o’erthrown with ceaseless Venom spread, Still hiss out Scandal from their Hydra Head,
the long-necked geese of the world that are ever hissing dispraise […]

s.def: To emit or eject (something) with a hissing sound.
ex: The man in white pyjamas hissed soda into his glass.
The radiator bubbled and hissed steam.
He hissed air intently through a gap in his upper teeth.

s.def: To whisper, especially angrily or urgently.
ex: "Are you quite sure of it," she hissed into his ear, "Mr Fang, Junior?"
"Oh please," she said, "don't let him see us!" I wouldn't let her push me away. "Stop!" she hissed. "He'll see us!"

s.def: An utterance used to discreetly attract someone's attention.
An injunction to be silent and/or to pay attention to what is being said or can be heard.
ex: There’s a clue somewhere; wait a bit; hist—hark! By Jove, I have it!

s.def: An instance of an exclamation attracting attention or injunction to be silent.
Abbreviation of history.
Pronunciation spelling of hoist.

s.def: An amine, C₅H₉N₃, formed by decarboxylation of histidine, that causes dilatation of capillaries, contraction of smooth muscle, and stimulation of gastric acid secretion; it is released during allergic reactions.
ex: The intake of food triggers a release of histamine, which activates the acid-secreting cells.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- Ancient Greek ῐ̔στός (hĭstós)bor. English histo- English -idine English histidine From histo- + -idine.

s.def: An essential amino acid C₆H₉N₃O₂ found in most animal proteins; essential for tissue growth and repair.

ety: From histo- + -logy.

s.def: The study of the microscopic structure, chemical composition and function of the tissue or tissue systems of plants and animals.
ex: Holonym: cytohistology

s.def: A lung disease caused by a fungus, Histoplasma capsulatum, often asymptomatic otherwise with symptoms similar to those of flu.

ety: From Middle English historian, historien, from Old French historien, from Latin historia (“story, history”), equivalent to histor(y) + -ian. More at history.

s.def: A writer of history.
One who studies or researches history.
ex: If this is what real people and societies are like, then it may be appropriate for historians to represent their subjects' lives in storylike form.
history does not consult the convenience of historians, though some of them are not always aware of it.

s.def: One who recounts their own medical history.
ex: The patient is unconscious when the syncopal event takes place and therefore is a poor historian.

s.def: Very important; noteworthy: having importance or significance in history.

the historic moment when the Berlin Wall came down, together with the preservation of the city's historic district

s.def: Old-fashioned, untouched by modernity.
ex: Sights are thick sown in the counties of York and Nottingham: the former is more historic.

s.def: Synonym of historical: of, concerning, or in accordance with recorded history or the past generally (See usage notes.)
ex: An high-pac'd Muse treading a lofty march, leades honor enchaind in an Epique pen, grac'd with the furtherance of historique Clio.

s.def: Various grammatical tenses and moods specially used in retelling past events.
ex: The historic tenses include the imperfect, the pluperfect, and the future perfect.

s.def: A history, a non-fiction account of the past.
A historian.

ety: From Latin historicus (“historical”) + -al (forming adjectives denoting of or relating to). By surface analysis, history + -ical.

s.def: pertaining to history
Of, concerning, or in accordance with recorded history, (particularly) as opposed to legends, myths, and fictions.
ex: July 4, 1776, is a historic date. A great deal of historical research has been done on the events leading up to that day.
The historical works of Lord Macaulay and Edward Gibbon are in and of themselves historic.
an important historical personage

s.def: Of, concerning, or in accordance with the past generally.
ex: The historical present is often treated as a principal tense, but there are exceptions and sometimes both constructions appear in the same passage.

ex: The Royal Historical Society
The State Historical Society of Wisconsin

s.def: Forming compound adjectives with the meaning "historical/~" or "historically"
ex: historical-political

s.def: A historical romance.

ety: Calque of German historischer Materialismus. Its earliest extant attestation - in German - is in Friedrich Engels's letter [5 August 1890] to Conrad Schmidt. Its earliest extant public attestation - in English - is in Engels's 1892 "Introduction to the English Edition" to his 1880 booklet Socialism: Utopian and Scientific.

s.def: A methodological approach to the study of society, economics, and history, looking for the causes of developments and changes in human society in the means by which humans collectively produce the necessities of life.

ety: From historical + -ly or historic + -ally.

s.def: In a historic manner; with reference to history or the historical record.
ex: Historically speaking, this company has always collected payment before starting work.
The law will prove to be historically significant.
Virtually all modern scholars of antiquity agree that Jesus existed historically.

s.def: According to history: formerly, in the past, traditionally.
ex: Historically, this company collected payment before starting work.
Historically, a rise in interest rates slows the rate of inflation.
Holden Matthews, 21, has been charged in connection with fires at three historically black churches in Louisiana.

s.def: To an unprecedented or extremely rare degree.

ety: Probably from French historicité, or from Latin historicus + -ity. Equivalent to historic + -ity.

s.def: Historical quality or authenticity based on fact.
ex: The historicity of minor political figures of this period is often hard to establish due to a dearth of sources.

s.def: The characteristic of having appeared or developed in history, as opposed to being natural or universal.
ex: This particular school places great emphasis on the historicity of ideas, practices, or institutions.

ety: From historiography + -er.

s.def: A scholar who studies historiography.
ex: "That's a fine young fellow," said the historiographer of earwigs, to an American who stood next him in the crowd.

ex: As was mentioned on p.31, value-judgments are generally considered the most conspicuous source of subjectivity in historiography.

s.def: The study of the discipline and practice of history and the writings of past historians.

s.def: The aggregate of past events, both unrecorded and recorded.
ex: The history of mammals stretches back many millions of years.
History repeats itself if we don’t learn from its mistakes.
He dreams of an invention that will make history.

s.def: The portion of the past that is known and recorded by this field of study, as opposed to all earlier and unknown times that preceded it.
ex: Near-synonym: ages
in all of human history and prehistory
since the dawn of history

s.def: A record or narrative description of past events.
ex: I really enjoyed Shakespeare's tragedies more than his histories.
a short history of post-Columbian colonization
Thucydides wrote a history of the Peleponnesian War that uses different sources than Herodotus' work.

s.def: A list of past and continuing medical conditions of an individual or family.
ex: A personal medical history is required for the insurance policy.
He has a history of cancer in his family.

s.def: A record of previous user events, especially of visited web pages in a browser.
ex: I visited a great site yesterday but forgot the URL. Luckily, I didn't clear my history.
When you do that, the browser window has no browser history, so it doesn't report a referrer page to the first site you visit.

s.def: Something that no longer exists or is no longer relevant.
ex: I told him that if he doesn't get his act together, he's history.

s.def: The empirical study of past events, as distinct from literature, myth, or scripture; the assessment of notable events.
ex: He teaches Latin American history at the university and publishes books about the Cold War.

ex: a long and sordid history

The family's history includes events best forgotten.

s.def: Shared experience or interaction.
ex: There is too much history between them for them to split up now.
He has had a lot of history with the police.

s.def: A historically significant event.
ex: You are witnessing history!
We have a new president: Barack Obama. I never thought a black man would be elected. It's exciting! It's history!

s.def: Things that have happened in the past will or tend to happen again in one way or another.

A personality disorder characterized largely by exaggerated emotions, and inappropriate attention-seeking and seductive behavior typically caused by undue amounts of trauma and related stress during childhood.
ex: Patients with histrionic personality disorder are sometimes accused of being attention whores.

s.def: to administer a blow — see also strike
A collision of a projectile with the target.
To strike.
ex: One boy hit the other.
He tried to hit me but I dodged the blow and went out to plot revenge.
I hunted him for half a hour, aiming to learn him to hit a man with a table-leg and then run, but I didn't find him.

ex: I hit the jackpot.
You can't hit the high notes in that song!

ex: Somebody's been here! Hit the lights!

ex: - I'd love to hear your band play. - Hit it, boys!

ex: We hit the grocery store on the way to the park.

s.def: To encounter an obstacle or other difficulty.
ex: You'll hit some nasty thunderstorms if you descend too late.
We hit a lot of traffic coming back from the movies.

s.def: To attain, to achieve.
ex: The movie hits theaters in December.
The temperature could hit 110°F tomorrow.
We hit Detroit at one in the morning but kept driving through the night.

s.def: To affect negatively.
ex: The economy was hit by a recession. The hurricane hit his fishing business hard.

s.def: To join a poker game, quickly win several hands, then leave.
To hit something or someone with a vehicle and leave the scene of the incident.
To engage in sexual intercourse followed by a prompt departure; to engage in a one-night stand.
ex: You can't hit and run / I've got to be number one / Better make up your mind / 'Cause you'll never find a love so divine

s.def: Synonym of pick and pass.
To download through peer-to-peer file sharing protocols (e.g., BitTorrent) without seeding.
To leave the base before the batter hits the ball.
To flirt with; to approach and speak to (someone), seeking romance, love, sex, etc.
ex: That's the third guy that has hit on her tonight.
Guys are hitting on them almost all the time.

ex: He hit on a great idea for improving the design.

ex: He was hit on his head so strongly that he stumbled forward and then he was severely hit from several sides.

ex: All characters have "hit points" that increase as they traverse the dungeon performing their brave deeds (unless they're smitten by some monster).
Damage reduces the monster's hit points; if the monster's hit points drop to 0, it's defeated.

ex: The in/out status for the hit point is determined by examining the loop which has the subelement (edge or vertex) closest to the hit point.

w: hit the nail on the head

s.def: To identify something exactly; to arrive at exactly the right answer.
ex: He hit the nail on the head when he said the problem was the thermostat.

ety: Probably from Middle English hicchen, hytchen, icchen (“to move; to move as with a jerk”), of obscure origin. Lacks cognates in other languages. Compare itch, hike.

s.def: A sudden pull.
Any of various knots used to attach a rope to an object other than another rope.
A fastener or connection point, as for a trailer.
ex: His truck sported a heavy-duty hitch for his boat.

s.def: A problem, delay or source of difficulty.
ex: The banquet went off without a hitch
The service operated according to plan on the Monday morning with only a few hitches.
Over the next week, the hitch in my dad's stride eased a bit. But we'd run out of things to talk about.

ex: The deal sounds too good to be true. What's the hitch?

ex: She served two hitches in Vietnam.

s.def: To pull with a jerk.
ex: She hitched her jeans up and then tightened her belt.

s.def: To attach, tie or fasten.
ex: He hitched the bedroll to his backpack and went camping.

ety: From hitch + hike.

s.def: To try to get a ride in a passing vehicle while standing at the side of a road, generally by either sticking out one's finger or thumb or holding a sign with one's stated destination.
ex: Holly came from Miami, F-L-A / Hitchhiked her way across the U.S.A.

s.def: To try to get (a ride) in this manner.
ex: Pamela hitchhiked a ride to New York.

s.def: To be carried along with something else.
ex: In genetic hitchhiking, a gene is propagated because it occurs in conjunction with a favourable mutation.
In cultural hitchhiking, a cultural trait spreads with a technologically advanced population.

An item attached to a travel bug and hidden in a geocache to be found and transported to other caches or around the world.
A dance move in which the dancer mimics the motions of someone thumbing a ride.
A bur that attaches and clings to clothing, or a bur-bearing plant.
An advertisement at the end of a program.
A post to which a horse (or other animal) may be tethered to prevent it from straying.
ex: Joe tied his horse to the hitching post before going into the bank.

s.def: A main shelter at a recreation place (e.g. a campground) where people go to socialize, eat, and purchase small items.
ex: The two girls who were camping went to the hitching post to buy some hot dogs and buns for the wiener roast.

Of or relating to the Hittite people.
Of or relating to the Hittite language.

w: how do I get to the train station

s.def: Used to ask for directions in order to go to a train station.

A greeting used upon being introduced to someone. Alternatives are how are you, pleased to meet you, and nice to meet you. (Sometimes used as a rhetorical question among familiar parties, depending on the region).
ex: ‘How do you do!’ said the Minister. ‘I’m very well, indeed! how’s yourself?’
"How do you do?" began Pollyanna politely. "I'm from Miss Polly Harrington, and I'd like to see Mrs. Snow, please."

ˈhaʊ duː ˈjuː pɹəˈnaʊns ðɪs ˈwɝd
