ety: Inherited from Old English hū maniġ.

s.def: what number
ex: How many of you have full-time jobs?
I've invited three hundred people to my wedding. — You've invited how many?
The message itself is neither difficult nor simple, but how many will realize this?

s.def: unspecified number
ex: We've lost quite a few; I don't know exactly how many.
And I saw how many were destroying the simplicity, and betraying the truth.
Biff then stated, “Take how many you want, they're $700 a piece."

w: how many languages do you speak

s.def: Used to ask the interlocutor how many languages he or she speaks.

w: how many siblings do you have

s.def: Used to ask how many brothers or sisters someone has.
What amount or quantity of (something stated or implied).
ex: How much (cheese) is left in the fridge? - This is how much we've got left.
How much of a problem will that cause the government?

s.def: What amount of money.
ex: How much do you want for it?
How much is it?
How much is it worth?

s.def: Used to ask a professional the monetary cost of his/her services.
Used to question the mental age (maturity) of the interlocutor.
ex: Jack: (laughing at infantile humor) Jill: How old are you?

s.def: Asks the age of the interlocutor.
ex: Literally: What is your age in years?

s.def: Used to inquire about the weather.
Indicating a change of subject to unimportant topics.

ety: Univerbation of how + be + it, literally “however it [may] be”.

s.def: Although.
Be that as it may; nevertheless.

ety: From Hindi हौदा (haudā), from Arabic هَوْدَج (hawdaj, “litter carried by a camel”) (1774).

s.def: A seat, usually with a canopy, carried on the back of an elephant or camel.
ex: They don't ask for palanquins and howdahs.
I shot a couple […] Only from the safety of a howdah, of course.

s.def: An ornate carriage which is positioned on the back of elephants or occasionally other animals, used most often in the past for rich people who travelled in India via elephant.

ety: Clipping of howdy-do, from how-d'ye-do (“how do you do”).

s.def: An informal greeting.
ex: Howdy folks, and welcome to our ninth annual chili cookoff!

s.def: To greet informally, especially by saying "howdy"
A wife.
A midwife.

ety: From Middle English however, how-ever, how-evere; equivalent to how + -ever. Compare howsoever.

s.def: In any way that one likes or chooses; in a haphazard or spontaneous way.
ex: I don't care; just do it however.
Nothing was really planned; things just happened however.

s.def: Nevertheless; yet, still; in spite of that.
ex: He told me not to do it. However, I did it anyway. / I did it anyway, however. / I, however, did it anyway.
She wanted to go; however, she decided against it.
I didn't argue with him; I still think, however, that he is wrong.

s.def: In contrast.
ex: The conference itself went very well. The party afterwards, however, was a disaster.

s.def: Regardless of how; no matter how
ex: However clear you think you've been, and however many questions you may've answered, there'll always remain some doubts.
Any rule of thumb, however true (it is), is useless unless you understand its underlying logic.
However much I study, I never get good grades.

s.def: Regardless of how; regardless of the way in which.
ex: Let me know when you've had your interview, however it goes.
However we do this, it isn't going to work.

s.def: In any way in which; how.
ex: She offered to help however she could.
Wear your hair however you want.

s.def: How ever: an emphatic form of how, used to ask in what manner.
ex: I thought it was impossible. However were you able to do it?

s.def: In any case, at any rate, at all events.
ex: Our chief end and highest interest is happiness : And this is happiness to be freed from all (if it may) [or] however from the greatest evils.

s.def: But, yet, though, although.
ex: *She wanted to go, however she decided against it.

ety: Borrowed from Dutch houwitser, from German Haubitze, from Middle High German haufniz, from Czech houfnice, which was derived from houf (“flock, crowd”) + -nice. The Czech noun houf comes from Middle High German hufe (“heap”), from Old High German hūfo.

s.def: A cannon that combines certain characteristics of field guns and mortars, delivering projectiles with medium velocities, usually with relatively high trajectories; normally a cannon with a tube length of 20 to 30 calibers.
A powerfully hit shot.
To attack with a howitzer.

ety: From Middle English howlen, houlen, from Old English *hūlian, from Proto-West Germanic *hūilōn, from Proto-Germanic *hūwilōną, *hiuwilōną (“to howl”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *kū-, *kew- (“to howl, scream”). Likely of imitative origin. Cognate with Saterland Frisian huulje (“to howl”), Dutch huilen (“to cry”), Romanian a hăuli (“to howl”), Old French ouler, German Low German hulen (“to howl”), German heulen (“to howl”), Danish hyle (“to howl”), Swedish yla (“to scream, yell”), Northern…

s.def: The protracted, mournful cry of a dog, wolf or other canid; also of other animals.
ex: [T]he fox was out on love-adventures, abused his rivals, and uttered scoffing screams and howls.
Dan was beginning to feel very depressed when suddenly the eerie howl of a dingo rang out[.]

s.def: Any similar sound.
ex: The howl of the wind

s.def: A prolonged cry of distress or anguish; a wail.
To utter a loud, protracted, mournful sound or cry, as dogs and wolves often do.
ex: Methought a legion of foul fiends / Environ'd me about, and howled in my ears.

s.def: To utter a sound expressive of pain or distress; to cry aloud and mournfully; to lament; to wail.
ex: Howl ye, for the day of the Lord is at hand.

s.def: To make a noise resembling the cry of a wild beast.
ex: They howled with laughter at the prank.
Wild howl'd the wind the forest glades along, / And oft the owl renew'd her dismal song; […]

s.def: To utter with outcry.
ex: to howl derision

ety: From howl + -er. Some senses are derivatives of the intensifier "howling", as in "howling wilderness", (Deuteronomy 32:10)

s.def: That which howls, especially an animal such as a wolf or a howler monkey.
A person hired to howl in mourning at a funeral.
A painfully obvious mistake.
ex: A howler is a glaring mistake, a mistake that cries out to be noticed.

s.def: A hilarious joke.
A bitterly cold day.
A person who expresses aggression openly in the form of threats.
A heavy fall.
A serious accident (especially to come a howler or go a howler; compare come a cropper).
ex: Our hansom came a howler.

s.def: A tremendous lie (especially an obvious one); a whopper.
ex: Trump has been trying to sell the howler that India offered a zero tariffs deal, when Modi isn’t even willing to take Trump’s repeated calls.

s.def: A fashionably but extravagantly overdressed man, a "howling swell".
A Central American and South American monkey of the genus Alouatta, noted for their loud call.

ety: From Middle English howsoevere, how-so-evere, how so evere. By surface analysis, how + so + ever.

s.def: Regardless of the way in which.
ex: Howsoever they pleaded, their pleas went unheard.

s.def: In any manner whatsoever.
ex: The party to this agreement may use the property whensoever and howsoever he or she pleases.

s.def: To whatever degree or extent.
ex: Their evidence, howsoever true it may have been, was not believed.

ety: From Hoxha + -ism, after Albanian leader Enver Hoxha.

s.def: A form of antirevisionist Marxism-Leninism.

ety: Borrowed from German Heu or Dutch gooi.

s.def: A small coaster vessel, usually sloop-rigged, used in conveying passengers and goods, or as a tender to larger vessels in port.
ex: Per packet per Hoy.
The hoy went to London every week.

s.def: Hey! ho!, hallo!, stop!
To incite; to drive onward.
To throw.
ex: They grab his duds and his picks as well. They hoy him down to the pit of hell. Down you go and fare ye well. You dirty blackleg miner.

ety: Probably from Middle Dutch heyden (“heathen, gypsy”), heidin (Modern Dutch heiden).

s.def: A rude, uncultured or rowdy girl or woman.
ex: Tabitha is lighting the candles in the sconces. A great, strong, heavy girl, a hoyden, not pretty, her face distinguished only by youth, by health.

s.def: Like a hoyden: high-spirited and boisterous; saucy, tomboyish.
To behave in a hoydenish manner.
Abbreviation of horsepower (unit of power).
ex: The ERS can generate an extra 160hp for around half a minute per lap.

s.def: Abbreviation of hour.
Initialism of horizontal rule.

ety: From Ukrainian гри́вня (hrývnja). Doublet of grivna and grzywna.

s.def: The currency of Ukraine, symbol ₴, divided into 100 kopiykas.
Initialism of Hypertext Markup Language.
Initialism of Hypertext Markup Language Version 5.

ety: From HTTP + magic cookie.

s.def: A packet of information sent by a server to a World Wide Web browser and then returned by the browser each time it accesses that server, used to maintain state between otherwise stateless HTTP transactions, for example, to identify the user.

ety: From earlier hubbe, which has the same immediate origin as hob. Hub was originally a dialectal word; its ultimate origin is unknown. Compare German Hubbel (“bump on a surface”), from Proto-West Germanic *hubil (“bump, hill”) (which contains a diminutive suffix *-il); compare English hive, or perhaps ultimately from the same root as hip or hop.

s.def: The central part, usually cylindrical, of a wheel; the nave.
ex: If you need to reload film, the cassette can be rewound slightly by turning the hub located on one end of its spool.

s.def: A point where many routes meet and traffic is distributed, dispensed, or diverted.
ex: Hong Kong International Airport is one of the most important air traffic hubs in Asia.

s.def: A central facility providing a range of related services, such as a medical hub or an educational hub.
A computer networking device connecting several Ethernet ports. See switch.
A stake with a nail in it, used to mark a temporary point.
A male weasel; a buck; a dog; a jack.
A rough protuberance or projecting obstruction.
ex: a hub in the road

s.def: An area in a video game from which individual levels are accessed.
A goal or mark at which quoits, etc., are thrown.
A hardened, engraved steel punch for impressing a device upon a die, used in coining, etc.

ety: In early use, the noun is often mentioned as a cry by Irish people, and so is possibly borrowed from Irish; compare Irish ababú, abú (“used as a battle cry”), and Scottish Gaelic ub, ub, ubub (“used to express contempt, etc.”), ubh ubh (“used to express disgust”). The verb is derived from the noun.

s.def: A confused sound of a crowd of people shouting or speaking simultaneously; an uproar.
ex: [T]he mighty Amsterdam, […] its Exchange resounding with the endless hubbub of all the languages spoken by civilised men.

s.def: Noisy confusion; commotion, uproar; (countable) an instance of this; an ado, a commotion.
ex: A scene of uproar and hubbub ensued that defies description.
The place will be in a fine hubbub, I suppose.
What's all the hubbub, bub?

s.def: A sound of people making a battle cry or war cry.
To make a confused sound of a crowd of people shouting or speaking simultaneously; to cause a racket or tumult.
Synonym of bowl game (“a Native American game of chance involving the throwing of colored nuts from a bowl, comparable to dice”).

ety: Diminutive of husband + -y.

s.def: Husband.
ex: Laura thought Jack was the most wonderful hubby in the world.

s.def: Full of hubs or protuberances.
ex: A road that has been frozen while muddy is hubby.

ety: From hub + cap.

s.def: A decorative and protective disk that covers the hub of a motor car wheel.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὕβρις (húbris, “insolence, sexual outrage”).

s.def: Excessive arrogance or pride, or presumption; originally (Greek mythology) toward the gods; a feeling of overwhelming and all-encompassing pride.
ex: Antitrust prosecutors target big companies that exude hubris.

s.def: A type of coarse, absorbent cotton or linen fabric used for making towels.

ety: From huck (from Middle English hoke (“hook”), hokebone, probably so called because of its round shape) + -le. See also hook.

s.def: The hip, the haunch.
ex: […] which approves a quick gathering up of his legs withoute pain, his huckle bones round and hidden, […]
At what time Don Quixote, who had very much bruis'd his Huckle-bone, with a Hipshot grace approaching the Lady fell upon his Knees […]

s.def: A bunch or part projecting like the hip.
A homosexual man.
ex: He’s not! He can’t be! There's never been a huckle in the Osbourne family, and we can trace our lineage all the way back to the Second World War.
Sorry ! Only into birds. Why not get yourself along to the SOL. Plenty of huckles there.

s.def: To apprehend or arrest.
ex: He was awakened by a couple of burly police officers and huckled out to a waiting van.
I could huckle your right now for what you've got in that top drawer.

s.def: Alternative form of huckle bone.

ety: From Middle English hukster, probably of Low German or Dutch origin, from Middle Low German höken (“to peddle”) or Middle Dutch hokester, itself from hoeken (“to peddle, bend, bear on the back”), all from Proto-Germanic *huk-, probably related to *hūkan- (“to squat”), from *hūkkan-, back-formed from the iterative *huk(k)ōn-, from Proto-Indo-European *kuk-néh₂, from *kewk- (“to curve, bend”) (also the source of English high). Compare hawkster. By surface analysis, huck + -ster.

s.def: A peddler or hawker, who sells small items, either door-to-door, from a stall, or in the street.
ex: drive those china hucksters from the doors

s.def: Somebody who sells things in an aggressive or showy manner.
One who deceptively sells fraudulent products; snake oil salesman.
Somebody who writes advertisements for radio or television.
To haggle, to wrangle, or to bargain.
To sell or offer (goods) from place to place, to peddle.
To promote or sell (goods) in an aggressive, showy manner.

ety: From Middle English *hudelen, alteration (due to hudels, hidels (“hiding place”), see hiddle) of *huderen, hoderen (“to cover; press together; huddle”), a frequentative form of Middle English huden, hiden (“to hide”), equivalent to hide + -le and/or hide + -er. Compare Low German huderken (“to brood; coddle; nurse; lull children to sleep”).

s.def: A small group of individuals in very close proximity to one another.
ex: It’s about as riveting as listening to a huddle of ents discuss the finer points of deciduous shedding.

s.def: A hesitation during play to think about one's next move.
A dense and disorderly crowd.
To crowd together.
ex: The sheep huddled together seeking warmth.

s.def: To curl one's legs up to the chest and keep one's arms close to the torso; to crouch; to assume a position similar to that of an embryo in the womb.
To get together and discuss a topic.
To form a huddle.
To crowd (things) together; to mingle confusedly; to assemble without order or system.
ex: Our adversary, huddling several suppositions together,[…]makes a medley and confusion.

s.def: To do, make, or put, in haste or roughly; hence, to do imperfectly; usually with a following preposition or adverb (huddle on, huddle up, huddle together).
ex: Huddle up a peace.
Let him forecast his work with timely care, / Which else is huddled when the skies are fair.
Now, in all haste, they huddle on / Their hoods, their cloaks, and get them gone.

s.def: To hesitate during play while thinking about one's next move.

ety: From Henry Hudson, an English sea explorer.

s.def: Canadian sea
A gulf officially in Nunavut, but also surrounded by Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec, Canada, a southern extension of the Arctic Ocean. A large body of saltwater in northeastern Canada.
A town in east-central Saskatchewan, Canada, previously named Hudson Bay Junction, a railway junction for a line to Hudson Bay.
A rural municipality, the Rural Municipality of Hudson Bay No. 394, which surrounds the Saskatchewan town.

ety: From Middle English hewe, from Old English hīew (“appearance, form, species, kind; apparition; hue, color; beauty; figure of speech”), from Proto-West Germanic *hiwi, from Proto-Germanic *hiwją (“hue, form, shape, appearance; mildew”), from Proto-Indo-European *kew-, *ḱew- (“skin, colour of the skin”) or *ḱey- (“grey, dark shade”). Cognate with Swedish hy (“complexion, skin”), Norwegian hy (“fluff, mold, skin”), Icelandic hégómi (“vanity”), Gothic 𐌷𐌹𐍅𐌹 (hiwi, “form, show, appearance”). Comp…

s.def: A color, or shade of color; tint; dye.
The characteristic related to the light frequency that appears in the color, for instance red, yellow, green, cyan, blue or magenta.
ex: In digital arts, HSV color uses hue together with saturation and value.

s.def: Character; aspect.
ex: This puts a completely different hue on the matter.

s.def: Form; appearance; guise.
A shout or cry.

ety: Probably an altered spelling of earlier *hough, represented by Scots hech (“to breathe hard, pant”). Compare also German hauchen (“to breathe”).

s.def: A heavy breath; a grunt or sigh.
ex: With a huff, he lifted the box onto the back of the truck.

s.def: A condition of anger, annoyance, disgust, etc.
One swelled with a false sense of importance or value; a boaster.
ex: Lewd, shallow-brained huffs make atheism and contempt of religion the sole badge [...] of wit.

s.def: The act of removing an opponent's piece as a forfeit for deliberately not taking a piece (often signalled by blowing on it).
To breathe heavily.
ex: The run left him huffing and puffing.

s.def: To say in a huffy manner.
To enlarge; to swell up.
ex: Bread huffs.

s.def: To bluster or swell with anger, arrogance, or pride; to storm; to take offense.
ex: This senseless arrogant conceit of theirs made them huff at the doctrine of repentance.

s.def: To treat with arrogance and insolence; to chide or rebuke rudely; to bully, to hector.
ex: You must not think to huff us.

s.def: To vex; to offend.

ety: From earlier hugge (“to embrace, clasp with the arms”) (1560), probably representing a conflation of huck (“to crouch, huddle down”) and Old Norse hugga (“to comfort, console”), from hugr (“mind, heart, thought”), from Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“mind, thought, sense”), cognate with Icelandic hugga (“to comfort”), Old English hyġe (“thought”) (whence high (Etymology 2)).

s.def: A close embrace, especially when charged with an emotion such as affection, joy, relief, lust, anger, aggression, compassion, or the like, as opposed to being characterized by formality, equivocation or ambivalence (a half-embrace).
A particular grip in wrestling.
To embrace by holding closely, especially in the arms.
ex: Billy hugged Danny until he felt better.
They hugged for what seemed like an eternity.

s.def: To stay close to.
ex: to hug the shore, to hug the coastline
Gourock also boasted a pier railway, although its pier hugged the shore rather than jutting into the bay.

s.def: To hold fast; to cling to; to cherish.
ex: We hug intellectual deformities, if they bear our names

s.def: To crouch; to huddle as with cold.
ex: They had a slight breast work, and they hugged down behind it and waited.
bright rocks whose stain of emerald or quartz shaft of shine the starfish hugged beneath the tide .
She put her feet on a rung and hugged down against her knees, making herself even smaller.

s.def: To cling closely together.

ety: From Middle English huge, from Old French ahuge (“high, lofty, great, large, huge”), of unknown origin. One theory derives it from an underlying Old French a hoge (“at height”), from a (“at, to”) + hoge (“a hill, height”), the latter from Frankish *haug or cognate Old Norse haugr (“hill”); both from Proto-Germanic *haugaz (“hill, mound”), from Proto-Indo-European *kowkós (“hill, mound”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *kewk-, whence also English high.

s.def: Very large.
Very strong, powerful, or dedicated.
ex: Both of my parents are huge supporters of animal rights.
After the children went to bed, the couple got into a huge argument.

s.def: Very interesting, significant, or popular.
ex: The band's next album is going to be huge.
In our league our coach is huge!

s.def: Alternative form of hugger-mugger.
Alternative form of hugger-mugger

ety: Attested from circa 1600. Compare Dutch hè (“huh”).

s.def: Used to express doubt or confusion.
ex: Huh? Where did they go?

s.def: Used to express amusement or subtle surprise.
ex: Huh! I'm sure I locked it when I left.

s.def: Used to reinforce a question.
ex: Where were you last night? Huh?

s.def: Used either to belittle the issuer of a statement/question, or sarcastically to indicate utter agreement, and that the statement being responded to is an extreme understatement. The intonation is changed to distinguish between the two meanings - implied dullness for belittlement, and feigned surpri…
ex: (belittlement) A: "We should go to an amusement park; it would be fun." B: "Huh."
(agreement) A: "Murder is bad." B: "Huh!"

s.def: Used to indicate that one did not hear what was said.
ex: Huh? Could you speak up?

s.def: Used to create a tag question.
ex: It's getting kind of late, huh?

s.def: Representing the sound of heavy breathing.
Representing a chuckling sound.
ex: Mr. [Lambert] Wilson says this with a soft chuckle, sounding a bit like huh huh huh.
Helen starts laughing, properly now. Huh-huh-huh.

s.def: A kiai, shouted as a limb is swung in attack.
ex: Shawn quickly turns around and punches the pale hand, yelling "Huh! Huh! Hi yah'! Huh! Get off me! Yeah!"
HUH-HUH, HI-YAH!

ety: Coined by Australian model Joan Anderson. Former trademark of Wham-O, which introduced the product in 1958.

s.def: A toy in the form of a large hoop which is twirled around various parts of the body, especially the waist.

ety: From Middle English hulk, hulke, holke (“hut; shed for hogs; type of ship; husk, pod, shell; large, clumsy person; a giant”) (probably reinforced by Middle Dutch hulk, huelc, and Middle Low German hulk, holk, hollek (“freighter, cargo ship, barge”)), from Old English hulc (“light ship; heavy, clumsy ship; cabin, hovel, hut”), from Proto-West Germanic *huluk, *hulik, from Proto-Germanic *hulukaz, *hulikaz (“something hollowed or dug out, cavity”), equivalent to hole/hollow + -ock. Cognate with O…

s.def: A large ship used for transportation; (more generally) a large ship that is difficult to manoeuvre.
A non-functional but floating ship, usually stripped of equipment and rigging, and often put to other uses such as accommodation or storage.
ex: They could see the lighthouse shining on Quarantine Island, and the green lights on the old coal hulks.

s.def: A large structure with a dominating presence.
A big (and possibly clumsy) person.
To reduce (a ship) to a non-functional hulk.
ex: No further additions were made to this group, and by 1729 the Rank was extinct (the last to be struck was the Ludlow, which had been hulked in 1719).

s.def: To temporarily house (goods, people, etc.) in such a hulk.
To move (a large, hulking body).
ex: A man with four children crowding like saplings around him whistles to wake up the elephant seal who has hulked his impossible body onto the beach.

s.def: To be a hulk, that is, a large, hulking, and often imposing presence.
ex: As the occupants stepped out, he hulked at them menacingly and asked them the traditional question. 'Can Ah help youse?'
The whoosh pushed John down, and as he fell, he turned to see the machine hulking over him, just meters away. “Shit!” he cried [...]

s.def: Of a (large) person: to act or move slowly and clumsily.
ex: After a while he hulked up to where Erland sat, putting his hairy fist on the table and watching the boy work.

s.def: To remove the entrails of; to disembowel.

ety: From Middle English hul, hulle, holle (“seed covering, hull of a ship”), from Old English hulu (“seed covering”), from Proto-Germanic *hul-, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide”); or possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kal- (“hard”). Compare Dutch hul (“hood”), German Hülle (“cover, wrap”), Hülse (“hull”); also Old Irish calad, calath (“hard”), Latin callus, callum (“rough skin”), Old Church Slavonic калити (kaliti, “to cool, harden”). For the sense development, compare Frenc…

s.def: The outer covering of a fruit or seed.
Any covering.
To remove the outer covering of a fruit or seed.
ex: She sat on the back porch hulling peanuts.

s.def: The smallest set that possesses a particular property (such as convexity) and contains every point of A; slightly more formally, the intersection of all sets which possess the specified property and of which A is a subset.
ex: The orthogonal convex hull of an orthogonal polygon is the smallest orthogonally convex polygon that encloses the original polygon.
holomorphically convex hull; affine hull; injective hull

s.def: The body or frame of a vessel, such as a ship or plane.
ex: Deep in their hulls our deadly bullets light, / And through the yielding planks a passage find.

s.def: To drift; to be carried by the impetus of wind or water on the ship's hull alone, with sails furled.
ex: We goe not, but we are carried: as things that flote, now gliding gently, now hulling violently, according as the water is, either stormy or calme.
[…] Thus hulling in The wild sea of my conscience, I did steer Toward this remedy, whereupon we are Now present here together:
In this virtuous voyage of life hull not about like the ark, without the use of rudder, mast, or sail, and bound for no port.

s.def: To hit (a ship) in the hull with cannon fire etc.

ety: Possibly a rhyming reduplication of halloo (used as a greeting or to catch attention; used in hunting to urge on pursuers), hilloa, hullo (variants of “hello”), and similar words.

s.def: A clamour, a commotion; a fuss or uproar.
ex: They made such a hullabaloo about the change that the authorities were forced to change it back.

s.def: To make a commotion or uproar.
ex: They roared, they danced, they hullaballoed, they pinched one another; they behaved like young savages – but I knew I had got them safe.
Ho, hullaballoing clan / Agape, with woe / In your beaks, on the gabbing capes!
Twitter broke the news, and soon enough, the media hullaballooed over this latest act of art vandalism.

ety: From Middle English hummen (“to hum, buzz, drone, make a murmuring sound to cover embarrassment”); akin to Dutch hommelen (“to bumble, buzz”), dialectal Dutch hommen (“to buzz, hum”), Middle High German hummen (“to hum”), probably ultimately of imitative origin.

s.def: To make a sound from the vocal cords without pronouncing any real words, with one's lips closed.
ex: We are humming happily along with the music.

s.def: To drone like certain insects naturally do in motion, or sounding similarly.
A hummed tune, i.e. created orally with lips closed.

And there fell a hush upon the gods when they saw that Māna rested, and there was silence on Pegāna save for the drumming of Skarl.

s.def: To rush, to gush.
ex: On the fluir, bluid an punch now hush't leyke a stream, […]
[…] water, far down below, roaring and hushing over the rocks, […]

s.def: To send forth a rush of water over (some ground) so as to clear off the soil and other materials overlying, and thus uncover or separate out, ore.
ex: [He] had promised … that he would have a stop put to the hushing process.

s.def: Water which has been used to clear the soil off of some (area of) rock or ore.
ex: The great cause of the scarcity of fish in this river is without doubt the "hush" coming down from the lead mines in the upper waters. […]

s.def: A part of a mine or quarry where ore is to be, or has been, excavated by an artificial flow of water.
A bribe to maintain secrecy (to prevent bad publicity or to prevent the discovery of a crime).
ex: The scandal was even greater when it was announced that hush money had been paid to keep the faulty products unannounced.

ety: Blend of hush + lullaby or hush + -a- (connective interfix) + by (“goodbye, as in bye-bye”).

s.def: hush and be still; a lull to sleep
ex: The night is fair, and the waves are still, And the wind is singing to you and to me In this lowly home beside the sea — Hushaby, sweet my own!

s.def: A lullaby used to soothe babies to sleep.
